  "entries": [
    {
      "result": "success",
      "replication_type": "close experiment",
      "original_url": "https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2006.10.001",
      "original_title": "High in the hierarchy: How vertical location and judgments of leaders' power are interrelated",
      "original_authors": "Giessner, Steffen R.; Schubert, Thomas W.",
      "original_year": "2007",
      "original_journal": "Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes",
      "description": "Original Study 3a claimed that describing a leader as powerful rather than powerless causes participants to place the leader's box higher in an organization chart; this was tested in the current paper's Study 1.",
      "citation_sentence": "In Study 3a of the same original paper (Giessner & Schubert, 2007), we had tested the reverse effect -namely whether describing a leader as powerful versus powerless would result in placing a box of this leader on a higher versus lower vertical position within an organization chart.",
      "gt_ambiguity": "clear",
      "notes": "The authors explicitly state that the preregistered Study 1 successfully replicated the main findings of the original study."
    },
    {
      "result": "failure",
      "replication_type": "close experiment",
      "original_url": "https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2006.10.001",
      "original_title": "High in the hierarchy: How vertical location and judgments of leaders' power are interrelated",
      "original_authors": "Giessner, Steffen R.; Schubert, Thomas W.",
      "original_year": "2007",
      "original_journal": "Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes",
      "description": "Original Study 1a claimed that increasing the magnitude of the vertical distance between a leader and subordinates in an organization chart increases perceived power; this magnitude claim was tested in the current paper's Study 2.",
      "citation_sentence": "Study 2: Following up on ManyLabs' replication failure with an adjusted paradigm of Study 1a, Giessner and Schubert (2007)",
      "gt_ambiguity": "clear",
      "notes": "Study 2 found no effect of magnitude of vertical distance while rank order was held constant, and the authors describe the original positive finding as a false positive. The novel rank-order hypothesis is not coded as a separate replication entry."
    }
  ]
}
